danish.title: Første epilog (1813–20) — Kapitel 14
paragraphs: Kort efter kom børnene ind for at sige godnat. De kyssede alle, huslærerne og guvernanterne nejede, og de gik ud. Kun den unge Nikolaj og hans huslærer blev tilbage. Dessalles hviskede til drengen, at han skulle gå ned.
»Nej, monsieur Dessalles, jeg vil bede min tante om at lade mig blive,« svarede Nikolaj Bolkonskij (prins Andrejs søn), også hviskende.
»Tante, lad mig venligst blive,« sagde han og gik hen til sin tante.
Hans ansigt udtrykte bøn, uro og henrykkelse. Grevinde Marja så på ham og vendte sig mod Pierre.
»Når du er her, kan han ikke rive sig løs,« sagde hun.

»Jeg bringer ham til Dem om et øjeblik, monsieur Dessalles. Godnat!« sagde Pierre og gav den schweiziske huslærer hånden, hvorefter han vendte sig mod den unge Nikolaj med et smil. »Vi to har jo slet ikke set hinanden endnu... Hvor han ligner, Marja!« tilføjede han henvendt til grevinde Marja.
»Ligner min far?« spurgte drengen, blodrød i ansigtet, og så op på Pierre med strålende, henrykte øjne.

Pierre nikkede og fortsatte med det, han havde sagt, da børnene afbrød dem. Grevinde Marja satte sig med sit håndarbejde; Natasja (Pierres hustru) lod ikke sine øjne vige fra sin mand. Nikolaj og Denisov rejste sig, bad om deres piber, røg, hentede mere te fra Sonja — som sad træt men standhaftig ved samovaren — og udspurgte Pierre. Den krøllede, spinkle dreng sad med strålende øjne ubemærket i et hjørne, rykked en gang imellem til og mumlede noget for sig selv, tydeligvis grebet af en ny og stærk følelse, mens han vendte sit krøllede hoved med den tynde hals, blottet af den nedfaldne krave, mod det sted, hvor Pierre sad.

Samtalen drejede sig om det aktuelle sladder om magthaverne, hvori de fleste ser den vigtigste del af den indenrigske politik. Denisov, der var utilfreds med regeringen på grund af sine egne skuffelser i tjenesten, hørte med glæde om de ting, der foregik i Petersborg, som forekom ham dumme, og fældede kraftige og skarpe domme over det, Pierre fortalte dem.

»Før skulle man være tysker — nu skal man danse med Tatárinova og madame Krüdener og læse Eckartshausen og brødrene! Nej, de skulde bare slippe den fine fyr Bonaparte løs — han ville drive alt det nonsens på flugt! Tænk at give kommandoen over Semjonovregimentet til en fyr som den Schwartz!« udbrød han.

Nikolaj, som ikke delte Denisovs tilbøjelighed til at finde fejl ved alt, mente dog også, at diskussion om regeringen var en meget alvorlig og vægtig sag, og det faktum, at A var blevet udnævnt til minister for dette og B til generalguvernør for hint, og at kejseren havde sagt sådan og ministeren sådan, forekom ham meget vigtigt. Og derfor mente han, det var nødvendigt at interessere sig for disse ting og spørge Pierre ud. Spørgsmålene fra disse to holdt samtalen i sit vanlige spor af sladder om de højere regeringskredse.

Men Natasja, der kendte alle sin mands vaner og tanker, så, at han længe havde ønsket, men ikke kunnet dreje samtalen over i et andet spor og give udtryk for sin egen dybtfølte idé, som var grunden til, at han var rejst til Petersborg for at rådslå med sin nye ven fyrst Fjodor, og hun hjalp ham ved at spørge, hvordan hans sager med fyrst Fjodor var gået.
»Hvad handlede det om?« spurgte Nikolaj.

»Altid det samme,« sagde Pierre og så sig omkring på sine tilhørere. »Alle kan se, at tingene går så dårligt, at det ikke kan fortsætte sådan, og at det er alle anstændige menneskers pligt at modvirke det, så godt de kan.«
»Hvad kan anstændige mennesker gøre?« spurgte Nikolaj med let rynkede bryn. »Hvad kan der gøres?«
»Jamen, dette...«
»Kom ind i mit arbejdsværelse,« sagde Nikolaj.

Natasja, som længe havde ventet at blive kaldt ind for at amme sin baby, hørte nu ammen kalde og gik til børneværelset. Grevinde Marja fulgte efter hende. Mændene gik ind i arbejdsværelset, og den lille Nikolaj Bolkonskij fulgte efter dem, ubemærket af sin onkel, og satte sig ved skrivebordet i et skyggefuldt hjørne ved vinduet.
»Nå, hvad ville du gøre?« spurgte Denisov.
»Altid et eller andet fantastisk,« sagde Nikolaj.

»Jamen, det er sådan,« begyndte Pierre, idet han ikke satte sig, men gik frem og tilbage i rummet, af og til standsede brat, gestikulerede og læspede: »situationen i Petersborg er denne: kejseren ser ikke til noget. Han har helt overladt sig til denne mystik« (Pierre kunne ikke udstå mystik hos nogen nu). »Han søger kun fred, og kun disse mennesker sans foi ni loi — uden tro eller lov — kan give ham den — mennesker, der hensynsløst hugger og kvæler alt — Magnitskij, Araktjejev og tutti quanti... Du vil da give mig ret i, at hvis du ikke selv så til dine godser, men blot ønskede et roligt liv, jo barskere din forvalter var, desto lettere ville du nå dit mål,« sagde han til Nikolaj.
* Uden tro eller lov.
»Godt, men hvad fører det hen?« sagde Nikolaj.

»Jamen, alt er ved at gå til grunde! Røveri i retssalene, i hæren intet andet end prygl, eksercits og militærkolonier; folket pines, oplysning undertrykkes. Alt, hvad der er ungt og ærligt, knuses! Alle kan se, at det ikke kan fortsætte. Alt er spændt til en sådan grad, at det uundgåeligt vil briste,« sagde Pierre (som de, der gransker enhver regerings handlinger, altid har sagt, lige siden der fandtes regeringer). »Jeg sagde dem blot én ting i Petersborg.«
»Sagde hvem?«

»Du ved godt hvem,« sagde Pierre med et betegnende blik under brynene. »Fyrst Fjodor og alle de andre. At opmuntre kultur og velgørenhed er jo alt sammen udmærket. Målet er fortræffeligt, men under de nuværende omstændigheder kræves der noget andet.«
I det øjeblik bemærkede Nikolaj sin nevøs tilstedeværelse. Hans ansigt formørkedes, og han gik hen til drengen.
»Hvorfor er du her?«

»Hvorfor? Lad ham være,« sagde Pierre, greb Nikolaj i armen og fortsatte. »Det er ikke nok, sagde jeg til dem. Der kræves noget mere. Når man står og venter på, at den overspændte streng skal springe hvert øjeblik, når alle venter den uundgåelige katastrofe, så må så mange som muligt slutte sig sammen, så tæt de kan, for at modstå den almene ulykke. Alt, hvad der er ungt og stærkt, bliver lokket bort og fordærvet. En lokkes af kvinder, en anden af æresbevisninger, en tredje af ærgerrighed eller penge, og de går over til den lejr. Ingen uafhængige mænd som dig eller mig er tilbage. Hvad jeg siger er: udvid rækkevidden af vores selskab, lad løsenet ikke blot være dyd, men også uafhængighed og handling!«
Nikolaj, som havde forladt sin nevø, skubbede irriteret en lænestol op, satte sig i den og lyttede til Pierre, mens han hostede misfornøjet og rynkede panden mere og mere.
»Men handling med hvilket mål?« udbrød han. »Og hvilken stilling vil I indtage over for regeringen?«

»En hjælpende stilling. Selskabet behøver ikke være hemmeligt, hvis regeringen tillader det. Det er ikke blot ikke fjendtligt over for regeringen, det er et selskab af ægte konservative — et selskab af gentlemen i ordets fulde forstand. Det handler blot om at forhindre en eller anden Pugatjov i at dræbe mine børn og dine, og Araktjejev i at sende mig til en militærkoloni. Vi slutter os sammen udelukkende for det offentlige vel og den almene sikkerhed.«
»Ja, men det er et hemmeligt selskab og altså et fjendtligt og skadeligt, som kun kan volde ondt.«

»Hvorfor? Gjorde Tugendbund, som reddede Europa« (man vovede dengang endnu ikke at antyde, at Rusland havde reddet Europa), »nogen skade? Tugendbund er et dydens forbund: det er kærlighed, gensidig hjælp... det er, hvad Kristus prædikede på Korset.«

Natasja, der var kommet ind under samtalen, betragtede sin mand med glade øjne. Det var ikke det, han sagde, der glædede hende — det interesserede hende ikke engang, for det hele forekom hende yderst simpelt, og hun havde vidst det hele tiden (det forekom hende sådan, fordi hun vidste, at det udsprang af Pierres hele sjæl) — men det var hans livlige og begejstrede udseende, der glædede hende.

Drengen med den tynde hals, der stak frem fra den nedfaldne krave — ham, alle havde glemt — stirrede på Pierre med endnu større og mere henrykt glæde. Hvert ord fra Pierre brændte sig ind i hans hjerte, og med en nervøs bevægelse af fingrene brækkede han ubevidst lakseglene og fjerpenene, som hans hænder fandt på onklens bord.
»Det er slet ikke det, I tror; men det var, hvad den tyske Tugendbund var, og det er, hvad jeg foreslår.«

»Nej, min ven! Den Tugendbund er jo meget godt for pølseæderne, men jeg forstår det ikke og kan ikke engang udtale det,« afbrød Denisov med høj og bestemt stemme. »Jeg er enig i, at alt her er råddent og forfærdeligt, men den Tugendbund forstår jeg mig ikke på. Hvis vi er utilfredse, lad os så lave vores eget oprør. Det er i orden. Je suis votre homme!«
* »Jeg er jeres mand!«

Pierre smilede, Natasja brød ud i latter, men Nikolaj rynkede panden endnu mere og begyndte at bevise over for Pierre, at der ikke var udsigt til nogen stor forandring, og at al den fare, han talte om, kun eksisterede i hans fantasi. Pierre hævdede det modsatte, og da hans åndsevner var større og mere opfindsomme, følte Nikolaj sig trængt op i en krog. Det gjorde ham endnu vredere, for han var fuldt overbevist, ikke ved logik, men ved noget i sit indre, der var stærkere end fornuften, om rigtigheden af sin holdning.

»Jeg vil sige dig dette,« sagde han, rejste sig og forsøgte med nervøst sitende fingre at sætte sin pibe i et hjørne, men opgav til sidst forsøget. »Jeg kan ikke bevise det for dig. Du siger, at alt her er råddent, og at et omvæltning er på vej: det ser jeg ikke. Men du siger også, at vores troskabsed er et betinget anliggende, og dertil svarer jeg: 'Du er min bedste ven, det ved du, men hvis du dannede et hemmeligt selskab og begyndte at arbejde mod regeringen — hvad den end måtte være — så ved jeg, at det er min pligt at adlyde regeringen. Og hvis Araktjejev befalede mig at føre en eskadron mod dig og hugge dig ned, ville jeg ikke tøve et øjeblik, men gøre det.' Og det kan du argumentere om, så meget du vil!«

En pinlig tavshed fulgte disse ord. Natasja var den første til at tale og forsvarede sin mand og angreb sin bror. Hendes forsvar var svagt og ubehjælpsomt, men hun nåede sit mål. Samtalen blev genoptaget og ikke længere i den ubehageligt fjendtlige tone fra Nikolajs sidste bemærkning.
Da de alle rejste sig for at gå ind til aftensmad, gik den lille Nikolaj Bolkonskij hen til Pierre, bleg og med strålende, lysfyldte øjne.
»Onkel Pierre, De... nej... Hvis far levede... ville han være enig med Dem?« spurgte han.

Og Pierre indså pludselig, hvilken særlig, selvstændig, kompleks og stærk tanke- og føleproces der måtte have foregået i denne dreng under samtalen, og idet han mindedes alt, hvad han havde sagt, fortrød han, at drengen havde hørt ham. Han var dog nødt til at give ham et svar.
»Ja, det tror jeg,« sagde han modvilligt og forlod arbejdsværelset.
Drengen så ned og syntes nu for første gang at bemærke, hvad han havde gjort ved tingene på bordet. Han blev blodrød og gik hen til Nikolaj.
»Onkel, tilgiv mig, det var mig der... ubevidst,« sagde han og pegede på de itubrudte laksegl og fjerpenne.
Nikolaj rykked vred til.
»Nå ja, nå ja,« sagde han og kastede stumperne under bordet.
Og tydeligvis med besvær undertrykkende sin irritation vendte han sig bort fra drengen.
»Du burde slet ikke have været her,« sagde han.

english.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: Soon after this the children came in to say good night. They kissed everyone; the tutors and governesses made their bows and went out. Only young Nicholas and his tutor Dessalles remained. Dessalles whispered to the boy to come downstairs.
"No, Monsieur Dessalles, I'll ask my aunt to let me stay," replied young Nicholas Bolkonsky, also in a whisper.
"Auntie, please let me stay," he said, going up to his aunt.
His face showed entreaty, excitement, and a kind of ecstasy. Countess Mary glanced at him and turned to Pierre.
"When you're here he can't tear himself away," she said.

"I'll bring him to you shortly, Monsieur Dessalles. Good night!" said Pierre, giving his hand to the Swiss tutor, and he turned to young Nicholas with a smile. "You and I haven't had a chance to talk yet... How like his father he's getting, Mary!" he added, turning to Countess Mary.
"Like my father?" the boy asked, blushing crimson and looking up at Pierre with bright, enraptured eyes.

Pierre nodded and went on with what he had been saying when the children interrupted. Countess Mary sat doing needlework; Natasha kept her eyes fixed on her husband. Nicholas and Denisov got up, asked for their pipes, smoked, fetched tea from Sonya—who sat wearily but stubbornly at the samovar—and asked Pierre questions. The curly-headed, sickly boy with his shining eyes sat unnoticed in a corner, turning his curly head with its delicate neck, poking out of his turndown collar, toward Pierre. Every now and then he would shiver and murmur something to himself, clearly experiencing some powerful new feeling.

The conversation turned to the current political gossip in which most people see the chief interest of domestic politics. Denisov, dissatisfied with the government because of his own career disappointments, was delighted to hear of the foolish things being done in Petersburg, and commented on Pierre's words in sharp, biting terms.

"Before, you had to be German—now you have to dance with Tatarinova and Madame Krudener, and read Eckhartshausen and the rest of that brotherhood. They should just let that fellow Bonaparte loose—he'd knock all this nonsense out of them! Can you imagine—giving command of the Semyonovsky regiment to a man like Schwartz!" he cried.

Nicholas, who didn't share Denisov's readiness to find fault with everything, also thought that discussing the government was very serious and weighty business, and the fact that A had been appointed Minister of This and B Governor General of That, and that the Emperor had said such-and-such and the minister something else, all seemed very important to him. And he thought it was his duty to take an interest in it and to question Pierre accordingly. Between them, their questions kept the talk to the usual gossip about people high up in government.

But Natasha, who knew all her husband's ways and ideas, could see that he had been wanting for some time—but unable—to steer the conversation to a different subject and express his own deeply felt idea, the one he'd gone to Petersburg to discuss with his new friend Prince Theodore. And she helped him with a question: what was his business with Prince Theodore about?
"What was it about?" asked Nicholas.

"Always the same thing," said Pierre, looking around at his listeners. "Everyone can see that things are going so badly they can't be allowed to continue, and that it's the duty of every decent person to fight against it as best they can."
"What can decent people do?" Nicholas asked, frowning slightly. "What can be done?"
"Well, this—"
"Come into my study," said Nicholas.

Natasha, who had long been expecting to be called to nurse the baby, now heard the nurse calling and went to the nursery. Countess Mary followed her. The men went into the study, and young Nicholas Bolkonsky slipped in after them unnoticed by his uncle and sat down at the desk in a dark corner by the window.
"Well, what would you do?" asked Denisov.
"Always some wild scheme," said Nicholas.

"Well, here it is," began Pierre, not sitting down but pacing the room, sometimes stopping short, gesturing, and speaking with a slight lisp. "The situation in Petersburg is this: the Emperor doesn't look into anything. He's surrendered himself entirely to mysticism." (Pierre could not forgive mysticism in anyone now.) "All he asks is peace, and the only people who can give him peace are the people who have no conscience, no honor—Magnitsky, Arakcheyev, and the rest. You'll agree that if you didn't look after your estates and only wanted peace, the more ruthless your steward was, the sooner you'd get it," he said, turning to Nicholas.
* Without faith or law.
"Well, what does that lead to?" said Nicholas.

"Well, everything is falling apart! Corruption in the courts; in the army, nothing but flogging, drilling, and Military Settlements. The people are tortured; enlightenment is crushed. Everything young and honest is being destroyed! Everyone can see this can't go on. The string is stretched too tight and must break," said Pierre—as people examining the actions of any government have always said, since governments first existed. "I told them one thing in Petersburg."
"Told whom?"

"Well, you know whom," said Pierre, with a meaningful look from under his brows. "Prince Theodore and the others. Encouraging culture and philanthropy is all very well, of course. The aim is excellent, but in the present circumstances something else is needed."
At that moment Nicholas noticed his nephew's presence. His face darkened and he went up to the boy.
"Why are you here?"

"Leave him be," said Pierre, taking Nicholas by the arm and continuing. "That's not enough, I told them. Something more is needed now. When you stand waiting for the overstrained string to snap at any moment, when everyone is expecting the inevitable catastrophe—as many people as possible must join hands as tightly as they can to resist the general disaster. Everything young and strong is being lured away and corrupted. One is tempted by women, another by honors, a third by ambition or money, and they go over to that camp. There's no independent, free people left, like you and me. I say: broaden the scope of the society; let the watchword be not just loyalty to the emperor and virtue, but independence and action."
Nicholas had left his nephew, irritably pushed an armchair into place, sat down, and listened to Pierre, coughing with displeasure and frowning more and more.
"But action toward what goal?" he cried. "And where do you stand in relation to the government?"

"We'd be assistants. The society needn't be secret if the government allows it. Far from being hostile to the government, it's a society of true conservatives—gentlemen in the full sense of the word. It exists only to prevent Pugachev from coming to slaughter my children and yours, and to prevent Arakcheyev from shipping me off to a military settlement. We join together with the single aim of the common good and general safety."
"Yes, but it's a secret society and therefore hostile and harmful, and can only cause trouble."

"Why? Did the Tugendbund, which saved Europe"—at that time no one yet ventured to say Russia had saved Europe—"do any harm? The Tugendbund is an alliance of virtue: it is love, mutual aid... it is what Christ preached on the Cross."

Natasha, who had come in during the conversation, looked joyfully at her husband. It wasn't what he was saying that pleased her—that didn't even interest her, because it all seemed extremely simple and she had known it all long ago (it seemed so to her because she knew the source it all came from—Pierre's whole soul). What delighted her was his animated, enthusiastic appearance.

The boy with the thin neck sticking out of his turndown collar—whom everyone had forgotten—gazed at Pierre with even greater rapturous joy. Every word of Pierre's burned into his heart, and with a nervous movement of his fingers he unconsciously broke the sealing wax and quill pens on his uncle's desk.
"It's not at all what you think. That's what the German Tugendbund was, and what I'm proposing."

"No, my friend! The Tugendbund is all very well for the sausage-eaters, but I don't understand it and can't even pronounce it," Denisov broke in with a loud, determined voice. "I agree that everything here is rotten and horrible, but the Tugendbund I don't understand. If you're not happy with things—a rebellion, now that I can understand! Count me in!"
* "I'm your man."

Pierre smiled; Natasha began to laugh; but Nicholas knitted his brows still more and set about proving to Pierre that no great upheaval was in the offing, and that all the danger Pierre spoke of existed only in his imagination. Pierre argued the opposite, and since his intellectual powers were greater and more resourceful, Nicholas soon felt at a loss. This made him still angrier, for he was inwardly aware that—not by reason but by something stronger than reason—the rightness of his view was beyond question.

"I'll tell you this," he said, standing up and trying with nervously twitching fingers to prop his pipe in a corner, finally giving up the attempt. "I can't prove it to you. You say everything here is rotten and there's going to be a revolution. I don't see it. But you also say the oath of allegiance is a conditional thing—and to that I reply: you're my best friend, you know that, but if you formed a secret society and started working against the government—whatever kind it might be—I'd know it was my duty to obey the government. And if Arakcheyev ordered me to lead a squadron against you and cut you down, I wouldn't hesitate for a second. Make of that what you will!"

An awkward silence followed. Natasha was the first to speak, defending her husband and attacking her brother. Her defense was weak and clumsy, but it achieved its purpose. The conversation resumed, no longer in the unpleasantly hostile tone of Nicholas's last words.
When they all got up to go in to supper, young Nicholas Bolkonsky went up to Pierre, pale and with shining, radiant eyes.
"Uncle Pierre, you... no... If Papa were alive... would he agree with you?" he asked.

And Pierre suddenly realized what a powerful, independent, and complex process of thought and feeling must have been going on inside this boy during the conversation. Remembering everything he had said, he regretted that the boy had heard him. He had to give an answer, however.
"Yes, I think so," he said reluctantly, and left the study.
The boy looked down and seemed for the first time to notice what he had done to the things on the desk. He flushed and went up to Nicholas.
"Uncle, forgive me—I did that... by accident," he said, pointing to the broken sealing wax and pens.
Nicholas started angrily.
"All right, all right," he said, throwing the pieces under the table.
And clearly suppressing his annoyance with difficulty, he turned away from the boy.
"You shouldn't have been here at all," he said.
